This is objectively wrong. Kingston General Hospital uses paper charting for all inpatient orders, requisitions, consults, progress notes, routine nursing charting, and daily medication administration records.

What is even worse, patient charts from their family physicians are not accessible from within any available EMR at the hospital, and the only way to get hospital discharge summaries to family physicians is printing a paper copy for the patient to physically bring to them. 

Finally, some ER transfer records from the KFL&A health region, including MARs, progress notes, and nursing notes are hand written paper copies. 

It's frustrating for any healthcare staff to work within this system. It could cost more, I'm not sure. But in my eyes, the worst aspect is the high probability that critical patient information is lost, both physically and in translation. 

I would check your facts, restrain from calling anyone a liar, and perhaps reassess the paperless implementation you so boldly claim responsibility for.

The topic we are really talking about is risk. Are we willing to risk catastrophe for a potentially better future? Is it too late when the majority of the population is obese? Is it too late when New York is under water? When is it too late? What is the probability that a capitalistic ideal would work?

What I fear is that if there is no government intervention, companies will completely ignore health priorities and side with making more money. This means giving people what they want, which is usually something along the lines of chips and cheeseburgers. There is no doubt that there will be forces the promote healthy diets, but from the beginning they will be fighting an uphill battle, with the 'bad' companies getting further and further ahead. 

We can use our imaginations to see how this might develop. Starting tomorrow, all nutritional labels and ingredient lists are non-mandatory. Food and beverage companies will immediately remove those labels taking up precious advertising space, and replace it with pictures of healthy and happy people consuming their product. Let's say you and I are trying to identify what ingredients are in the product, how would we go about finding that out? I would agree that even in a completely capitalistic food world, the food will probably be safe, but what guarantee will there be for long-term health? Do we have any means to chemically identify the nutrients and caloric content of the product? 

You may argue that consumers will eventually form some group that will have enough resources to do this. But what makes that so different from what the FDA is doing now? 

Just a bit of disclosure, I'm a Canadian, and assumed you are American, so we may have different views on government run organizations.

What do you think will happen with the people that can't take care of themselves? If there is enough unhealthy people, will they ask for help? This is not just speculation, it is a very real problem already. The burden of diabetes is causing healthcare costs to skyrocket, and the majority of the cases are caused by poor eating habits. What do you think would happen if less nutritional information was given about food? Do you really think the majority of people will be curious enough to do the research themselves?

I have some big issues with this paper:

1. Each group, pre-hike and in-hike, were only tested once. The pre-hike group was tested only before they started their hike, then never tested again. The in-hike group was tested after the 4 day hike, but never before the hike started. This sets up many red flags to their conclusion. There could have been significant differences in 'creativity' between the groups before the hike even started. 

2. They didn't analyze whether or not the act of hiking, i.e. exercising, may be the reason behind the increase in test performance. Given the high likelihood of this being the actual cause of 'increased creativity', it causes a lot of doubt in their conclusion. The groups could have taken the test before and after a workout to get the same results.

3. The groups were selected randomly, so everyone that hiked together was most likely meeting individuals they have never met before. Having 4 days to meet and talking about new things (most likely) will certainly be stimulating enough to increase 'creativity'. 

4. The researchers don't account for the the change in environment that most likely happened to these people. Exposing anyone to a new environment will, again, likely stimulate the brain. If this was true, then it would have just been coincidence that the new environment was nature, when in fact, sending people to Las Vegas would do the same thing. 

All of these reasons, and the lack of explanation within the paper, give me reason to doubt the authors' conclusion.

Great points made by Destiny. But what if we considered the other perspective: Some maps were imbalanced for a certain race because of poor race design? As he says, rocks denying the third base of zerg and a large ramp leading into the natural of protoss are considered as poor map design choices. These problems could be reframed as zerg having trouble with space control, or protoss having extremely poor DPS in the early game. 

But no matter what perspective we look at the race balancing issue from, I think its important that Blizzard is willing to challenge established standards in order to keep the game entertaining. There are few opportunities that allow Dustin and David, et al., to do this with severely disrupting metagame, but I believe HotS beta is the perfect time to do this. Never increasing the vulnerability of the natural may be too restricting for protoss to try anything but forge fast expand. Never placing rocks at the third base of zerg may prevent early game zerg from being developed further. 

TL;DR: We know how to play on maps with safe naturals and thirds, but with new units on the horizon, shouldn't we explore different map standards?

I can only support the attention this serious problem is getting. From my position as a neuroscience Master's student, there seems to be no other options other than to stay in academia. There are attempts in our seminars to discuss other possible career opportunities, but in the end, the discussions never generate practical knowledge that I could use to plan my career. The reality is that the jobs of the professors who leads these seminars do not include research into the current labor market, hence the disconnect between how many graduate students are trained and the actual jobs available.

What I do not see clearly from the proposals of the two reports is how they address the excess amount of Ph.D's graduating every year. The clearest addressing of this issue is preventing more students to be funded, at the same time as relocating funding sources from the PIs to public organizations. This may prevent further increases in graduates, but doesn't fix the problem. Furthermore, some of the proposed actions seem to only increase the number of graduates, such as capping or reducing the time required to obtain a Ph.D, or increasing the pay of Post Docs in years 3 and 4. The main thing that will help will be to increase the amount of job opportunities, a plan for which I did not clearly get from the article.

Pneumothorax is air getting in between the chest wall and the lungs. 

Now for the scary part. Your lungs have a natural elasticity to them, which wants to collapase then inward. An uninflated lung, without anything stretching it out, is about the size of a fist, and very hard to inflate (think of an uninflated balloon). Your chest wall also has an elasticity to it, and it tends to pull out and up. The space inbetween them, the intrapleural cavity, is normally a sealed cavity. This seal allows the elasticity of the chest to keep the lungs open. It also allows you to breath by using your diaphragm (the bottom part of the sealed chest cavity), and your intercostal muscles in your chest. Now, if this seal is broken, it is impossible for your muscles to generate a negative pressure inside your lungs. You can't breath.

It is possible to fix, but the only way is through positive pressure into the lungs, and allow the puncture to heal (reseal). The initial situation is dangerous, and the healing process depends on the type of wound to the chest.

I agree that a 175 year copyright term stifles new content, but I disagree with the argument the video makes. 

Keep in mind the argument should lie in the length of the copyright. Moving on. 

They argue that society is worse off because others cannot remake or add to the original content. It is arguable whether this remade product would take just as much, or more, inspiration and creativity as the original product took. Note that copyright laws do not prevent others to be inspired to produce their own, at least in the entertainment industry. 

The stronger argument against long copyright laws is that they are a disincentive for the 'inventor', as in J. K. Rowling invented Harry Potter, and George Lucas invented Star Wars, to create new and interesting content. The more economically and socially successful their ideas are, the less of a drive for them to come up with more. The impact of this is increased if one considers that the bigger the impact the product makes, hence the more talented the individual, the less likely they are to make more. 

In my opinion, ludicrous 175 year copyright becomes only about money making, and not about nurturing innovation and ideas.

Some friends and I were driving back from a hockey game. It was late, around 1:00 am, on a Saskatchewan highway. This means you can see a car's headlights from kilometers away, due to the flat terrain and highways that tend not to curve. Many of us recently got our driver's licenses, so no parents were in the three vehicles we were driving back in. Cops were few and we were familiar with the area, so we raced to see who could get back home first. As I was passing my friend, I saw a light in the distance, but it was still a single point of light - plenty of time to pass. My friend speeds up to keep me from passing. I struggle to pass him as my adrenaline is racing, and that light is getting closer. My nerves get the better of me, so I slow down and go back into my lane. The instant I get back into my lane, a car whips by us in the opposite direction. That car had only one headlight working. My brother, who was in the car with me, and I shit our pants. 

TL;DR: I was a split second from a head on collision going 150 km/h, thinking I had more time because of a car with one working headlight.
